After almost eight years of taking something just to poop...

I sat in a gastroenterologist's office at 63 years old convinced she was about to tell me I had permanently damaged my colon.

That I had made it lazy.

That after years of Miralax, stool softeners, fiber and the occasional Dulcolax when I got desperate, my body had simply forgotten how to go on its own.

I had spent almost a year quietly worrying about it.

What she told me instead changed the way I looked at constipation completely.

And if you have been using something to make yourself go for years, especially if it seems like you need more help now than you used to, I think you will understand why I was so scared.

My name is Patricia.

I am 63 years old.

I have been married to my husband Michael for 37 years.

We have two daughters and four grandchildren.

My life is pretty ordinary.

I walk most mornings.

I garden when my knees cooperate.

I probably eat more bread than I should.

And until my late 50s, I never imagined I would spend so much of my life thinking about bowel movements.

It started around menopause.

At first I simply stopped going every morning.

Then it became every other day.

Then every third day.

Then came the little hard pellets.

If you deal with constipation, you know exactly what I am talking about.

You sit there for twenty minutes.

You push.

Maybe two or three little dry pieces finally come out.

Technically you went.

But you stand up feeling almost exactly as full as you did before.

That was me.

I mentioned it to my regular doctor and she suggested Miralax.

At first, it worked beautifully.

I would mix a capful into my coffee in the morning and usually sometime before lunch I would have a bowel movement.

I thought I had solved it.

After a while though, it became less predictable.

Some mornings it worked.

Some mornings it did not.

Then came fiber gummies. Prunes. Chia seeds. More water. Warm water. Coffee. One of those little stools you put under your feet while you are on the toilet.

And on the really bad weeks, Dulcolax.

I hated Dulcolax.

For me it would do absolutely nothing for hours, then sometime in the middle of the night I would wake up sweating with horrible cramps and spend the next hour in the bathroom.

At least I would finally go.

But three or four days later I would be right back where I started.

Bloated. Heavy. Passing little hard pieces. Never really feeling empty.

Eventually constipation became something I managed every single day.

Miralax in the morning. Fiber with lunch. Something stronger when I got badly backed up.

And for years I told myself that was simply how my body worked now.

Then one night I made the mistake of Googling:

"Can laxatives make your colon lazy?"

I wish I had not.

That one search sent me down a rabbit hole.

I found women saying they could not poop at all anymore unless they took something.

I read about slow transit. Colonic inertia. Impactions. Enemas. Surgery.

By about 3 in the morning I had convinced myself that I had ruined my own digestive system.

And once that thought got into my head, I could not shake it.

Every time Miralax did not work, I wondered if my colon was getting weaker.

Every time I needed Dulcolax, I wondered what I would do when that stopped working too.

That was the question that frightened me most.

What comes after this?

What happens when Miralax is not enough?

What happens when nothing is enough?

What happens when I am 70 and nothing works?

I also realized something that bothered me more than I expected.

I genuinely could not remember the last time I had simply felt a normal urge, gone to the bathroom, and had an easy bowel movement.

Everything had become something I had to manage.

I eventually brought all of this up with my regular doctor.

My bloodwork looked fine. My colonoscopy had been normal.

She told me constipation becomes more common as women get older.

Then came the same advice I had heard for years.

Keep using the Miralax. Drink plenty of water. Make sure you are eating enough fiber.

She was not rude about it.

But I left feeling defeated because I was already doing all of that.

I carried a water bottle around all day and somehow my poop still came out looking like it had been left in the sun.

Fiber often just made me feel more stuffed.

Miralax might give me one decent bowel movement and then two days later I would be back to rabbit pellets.

Nobody could tell me why.

A few months later I went four days with almost nothing despite everything I had taken.

I woke up one morning and my lower stomach felt hard and heavy.

Michael found me lying in bed with my hand over my abdomen.

He asked what was wrong.

And for the first time I actually said the fear out loud.

"I think I have broken my colon."

He knew I struggled with constipation. He had no idea how scared I had become.

That morning he told me we were going to find somebody who actually dealt with this all day instead of adding another bottle to my bathroom cabinet.

A few weeks later, I was sitting across from a gastroenterologist who spent a large part of her practice working with women with chronic constipation.

I went into that appointment expecting bad news.

Instead, she started asking questions about something no doctor had ever spent much time asking me about.

The poop itself.

What did it look like?

Usually little hard pellets.

Did I strain?

Almost every time.

Did I feel empty afterward?

Rarely.

Did increasing fiber help?

Not particularly.

Then she asked:

"When you do go, is the stool usually soft?"

I almost laughed.

No. Most of the time it was dry and hard. Sometimes little pebbles. Sometimes one bigger piece that felt like I was trying to pass a rock.

She pulled out a pad of paper.

Then she said something that reframed everything.

"Everybody focuses on how hard the colon is pushing. But that is rarely the problem. The problem is usually what has happened to the environment inside the colon."

She explained that a healthy colon has a thin mucus lining on the inside of its wall, produced by tiny cells called goblet cells.

That lining does two things.

It coats stool and helps it hold moisture so it stays soft and formed instead of drying into rock.

And it makes the inner wall of the colon slippery, so when the muscle contracts, stool actually glides forward instead of grinding against a dry surface.

She said: "When that lining is healthy, most women go every morning without even thinking about it."

Then she asked me something that stopped me cold.

"Did your constipation start around menopause?"

Yes. Absolutely.

She nodded like she had been expecting that answer.

She explained that estrogen directly feeds goblet cells and signals them to keep producing mucus. When estrogen drops during menopause, those cells lose their signal and mucus production collapses.

She said the same hormonal shift that dries out a woman's skin, eyes, and mouth after 50 also dries out the inside of the colon.

"You just cannot see it because it is happening inside your body."

Then she drew two shapes on the paper. A soft oval and a small hard circle.

She pointed to the first one.

"Imagine squeezing toothpaste through a tube."

Then she pointed at the second.

"Now imagine trying to push a dried-out cork through the same tube."

That was probably the first time constipation had been explained to me in a way that matched what I was actually experiencing.

For years I had assumed my colon was not pushing hard enough. So every time I got constipated, my instinct was to make it push harder. Another laxative. Something stronger.

But nobody had ever asked what condition the stool was in by the time my body was trying to move it. Or what had happened to the lining that was supposed to keep it soft.

Then I asked her something that had bothered me for years.

"If the problem is moisture, why am I still constipated when I drink water all day?"

She told me that was exactly the right question.

The water you drink does not travel through your body and soak the hard stool sitting at the other end of your digestive tract. Most of it is absorbed into your bloodstream much earlier and used throughout the body.

Meanwhile, your colon continues pulling moisture out of the stool already sitting there.

And without that mucus lining to regulate the process, it pulls out too much. The stool dries into cement. And no amount of drinking water changes that because the water never reaches where the problem is.

Then she explained why fiber had made me feel worse.

"Fiber creates bulk. But bulk only helps when there is enough moisture and lubrication to move it. If the lining is gone and the stool is already dry, adding more bulk is like adding more cars to a traffic jam. You are making the blockage bigger, not smaller."

I sat there thinking about every scoop of Metamucil I had choked down over the past six years.

Then she told me what she actually recommended for women in my situation.

She said there were three things my colon needed, and each one handled a different part of the problem.

The first was triphala extract.

She explained that triphala stimulates goblet cells directly and helps them start producing mucus again, even without the estrogen signal they used to depend on. She said research had found it restored the intestinal lining with effects on par with a prescription drug.

She told me this was the root cause piece. Without rebuilding the mucus lining, everything else was temporary.

The second was magnesium oxide.

She explained that this specific form of magnesium stays in the lower bowel instead of absorbing into the bloodstream like citrate or glycinate. Because it stays in the gut, it draws water directly toward the stool that has dried out and compacted.

She said: "Most magnesium supplements are designed to get into your blood. This one is useful precisely because it does not. It stays where the problem is."

The third was kiwifruit extract.

She said bringing water into the bowel was only half the job. If that moisture was not held inside the stool, the colon would just pull it right back out through the damaged wall.

Kiwifruit binds water into the stool at the gel level. She used a sponge as an example.

Pour water onto the counter and it runs everywhere. Put it into a sponge and the sponge holds onto it.

That was how she wanted me to think about magnesium oxide and kiwifruit together.

Magnesium brings the water in. Kiwifruit keeps the stool soft and hydrated instead of letting it turn right back into dry little rocks.

By the time she finished, she had three ingredients written on the page:

Triphala extract.

Magnesium oxide.

Kiwifruit extract.

Next to them she had written:

Rebuild the lining.

Bring water in.

Keep the stool soft.

I looked at the paper for a second and asked:

"Okay... where do I actually get these?"

She smiled.

"Funny enough, my sister takes a formula with all three."

That got my attention.

Her sister was in her late 50s and apparently had dealt with almost exactly what I was describing. Hard stools. Going every few days. That constant feeling that she had not completely finished.

So my gastroenterologist had explained the same three ingredients to her.

Her sister eventually found them together in one formula and had apparently been doing really well with it.

I asked what it was called.

She picked up her phone and searched through her messages for a moment.

Then she turned the screen toward me.

Regularity Reset.

"That is the one my sister takes," she said. "She has done really well with it."

Then she looked back at the three ingredients she had written down for me.

"If you want to try this approach, that is the formula I would look at."

She said what she liked about the combination was that each ingredient handled a different part of the problem.

The triphala rebuilds the mucus lining that menopause took away.

The magnesium oxide brings water directly to the stool.

And the kiwifruit holds that moisture in so the stool stays soft.

After everything she had just explained, it made perfect sense.

I also finally had a very different explanation for what had been happening to me than:

"You destroyed your colon."

My colon was not lazy. It was not broken. It was dry. The lining had disappeared after menopause and nobody had mentioned it until today.

I drove home with that little piece of paper sitting in my handbag.

That evening I looked up Regularity Reset.

Sure enough, the label had exactly what she had written down.

Triphala extract 300 mg. Magnesium oxide 500 mg. Kiwifruit extract 500 mg.

Everything matched what she had spent that appointment explaining to me.

For once, I actually knew why each ingredient was there instead of taking something because somebody on Facebook said it would "make me go."

So I ordered a bottle.

When it arrived, the directions said to take three capsules at night.

I started that evening.

I did not suddenly change everything else I had been doing for years. I was far too nervous for that.

I simply started taking the three capsules consistently and paid attention to what happened.

A few mornings later I noticed the first difference.

The stool itself was softer.

And I know that does not sound terribly exciting.

But after years of passing dry little pellets, it was the exact difference I had been hoping for.

It was formed, but it passed much more easily. I was not sitting there for twenty minutes trying to force something out of me.

Over the next week, that started happening more consistently.

Going to the bathroom gradually stopped feeling like such a production. I could sit down, go, and get on with my morning without all the straining I had gotten used to.

Then sometime during the second week, I was standing in the kitchen making coffee when I felt a normal urge.

That surprised me.

I was not painfully full and trying to make myself go because I knew it had been three days.

I simply needed the bathroom.

I went upstairs, had a bowel movement, and came back down to finish making coffee.

Michael asked why I looked so pleased with myself.

I said:

"I just went without having to think about it first."

He did not really understand why that was such a big deal. But I did.

By the third week, I noticed the heavy feeling in my lower stomach had eased too.

For years my pants would fit fine in the morning and feel tight by dinner.

If I had not gone in a couple of days, I would sometimes eat less because I hated thinking about adding more food on top of everything already sitting inside me.

I was not doing that anymore.

And when I did have a bowel movement, I was finally starting to get something I had almost forgotten about.

That feeling of being finished.

One Saturday morning I went to the bathroom and afterward my stomach just felt light.

There was not that familiar pressure telling me there was still more sitting there.

I walked into the kitchen and told Michael:

"I think I just pooped like a normal person."

He looked over his coffee.

"Well, congratulations."

I laughed.

But honestly, I was emotional about it.

Because people who do not deal with chronic constipation have no idea how much space it takes up in your head.

You know how many days it has been.

You think about whether you should eat a big dinner.

You wonder what you should take before bed.

You worry that whatever you take will suddenly kick in while you are away from home.

And when it goes on for years, you start wondering what is going to happen as you get older.

That was the part that had frightened me most.

I really believed I had spent eight years slowly making my colon weaker.

What the gastroenterologist gave me was a much simpler way of understanding what I was dealing with.

I had spent years asking:

"How do I make myself go?"

She got me thinking about another question:

"What happened to the lining that was supposed to keep my stool soft in the first place?"

Once I understood that the mucus lining had dried up after menopause, and that fiber was packing a dry pipe tighter, and that laxatives were destroying the goblet cells that could rebuild it, the whole problem finally made sense.

That is why the little note she wrote that day has stuck in my head.

Rebuild the lining.

Regularity Reset contains the exact three ingredients she recommended for doing those three jobs.

I still take three capsules at night.

And if you have been dealing with those dry little pellets...

Feeling like fiber just makes you even more full...

Or finding that the things you have relied on for years do not seem to work the way they used to...

I understand how frustrating that gets.

I also understand the thought that eventually starts creeping in:

That was the question running through my head at 1:17 in the morning, the night before my colonoscopy.

The bowel prep had done absolutely nothing for nearly two hours.

Then a piece of stool so large and hard came out that I screamed.

And once it moved...

Everything behind it started coming.

Load after load after load.

Every time I thought I was finished, another wave hit.

By the fourth trip, I was shaking.

By the tenth, I was staring into the toilet thinking:

Where the hell had all of this been hiding?

I hadn't eaten solid food all day.

And I had supposedly been "going" every three or four days.

So why did it look like my body had been holding onto weeks of waste?

"When was the last time you had a complete bowel movement without Miralax, Senna or Dulcolax?"

I opened my mouth to answer.

Why I could drink water all day and still pass dry rocks...

Why fiber made my stomach feel even bigger...

Why Miralax gave me results I could never predict...

And why the strongest laxatives only restarted the same miserable cycle.

Before menopause, I had always been regular.

I would have my coffee in the morning, use the bathroom and get on with my day.

I barely thought about it.

Then menopause came and my body seemed to change all at once.

The hot flashes started.

My sleep became terrible.

My waist thickened even though I wasn't eating differently.

And my digestion slowed to a crawl.

At first, I would skip one day.

Then two.

Eventually, I could go four or five days without what I would now call a proper bowel movement.

But I didn't tell anyone.

I was embarrassed.

Even with my husband, I would quietly take something and hope he didn't notice how often I disappeared into the bathroom.

I had Miralax in the kitchen cupboard.

Senna beside my bed.

Dulcolax in my handbag.

Fiber gummies in the car.

And a bottle of magnesium citrate hidden behind the towels for what I called "real emergencies."

My husband called it Linda's pharmacy.

I laughed whenever he said it.

But privately, I was scared.

Without something from that collection, my body barely did anything.

And when I finally did go, it was rarely normal.

Usually, three or four hard little pellets would drop into the toilet.

Sometimes they were so dry they left absolutely nothing on the paper.

Other times, one large piece would become stuck halfway out.

I would sit there rocking, sweating and pushing until my legs went numb.

"At least something came out."

That was how I convinced myself I wasn't really constipated.

I left it sitting on the bathroom counter for almost a month.

Partly because nobody enjoys collecting a stool sample.

My doctor said it could be hemorrhoids.

Every ache frightened me.

The day before my colonoscopy, I followed the preparation instructions exactly.

I stopped eating solid food.

I had broth, lemon gelatin and clear liquids.

At six that evening, I mixed the bowel preparation and drank the first portion.

Everyone had warned me to stay near the bathroom.

So I waited.

An hour passed.

Nothing.

Then another half hour.

Still nothing.

My stomach was bubbling and making awful noises.

I could feel liquid moving around inside me.

But I couldn't go.

I started panicking that I was going to fail the preparation and they would cancel my procedure.

Then I felt an enormous amount of pressure low down.

I rushed to the bathroom.

What came out first was not liquid.

It was one large, painfully hard piece of stool.

It felt like trying to pass a stone.

I gripped the edge of the sink and breathed through it.

My legs felt weak.

My backside was sore.

Actually empty.

I told her yes.

Then she asked what my final bowel movements looked like.

I said they were pale yellow and almost clear.

She nodded and said that was exactly what they wanted.

They put an IV in my hand.

The anesthesiologist told me to take a deep breath.

I had become a stranger in my own body.

More fiber. More bloating. More pressure. Bigger blockage.

Nobody had ever explained why.

This was the root cause piece. Without restoring the goblet cells and getting them producing mucus again, everything else was temporary.

She told me about a fruit extract called triphala that stimulates goblet cells directly and triggers them to start producing mucus again, even without the estrogen signal they used to depend on.

"Research found it restored the intestinal lining with effects on par with a prescription drug," she said. "And it doesn't irritate the colon wall the way laxatives do. It rebuilds what laxatives and menopause destroyed."

✅ Second, water had to be pulled directly into the colon where the stool is.

I went every single morning, like clockwork.

That heavy, backed up feeling I'd been carrying around for years was more than half gone, and for the first time in ages my pants buttoned all the way up at 8pm.

I could feel the brain fog starting to lift too. I was sharper and quicker, more like the woman I used to be at 40.

The constant low grade headache I'd had for the last 4 years was gone. My joints stopped aching, and my energy came roaring back.

And I stopped thinking about it, which sounds like a small thing but isn't. For six years, my very first thought every morning was whether today was going to be a bad day.

That thought just stopped showing up.

Dr. Chen had given me her office number before I left the hospital and asked me to call and let her know how I got on.

I told her I was going every morning, on my own, with no laxatives at all. That nothing hurt. That my stomach was soft again.

I felt 30 years old again.

I walk most mornings.

It started around menopause.

At first I simply stopped going every morning.

Then it became every other day.

Then every third day.

Then came the little hard pellets.

If you deal with constipation, you know exactly what I am talking about.

You sit there for twenty minutes.

You push.

Maybe two or three little dry pieces finally come out.

Technically you went.

But you stand up feeling almost exactly as full as you did before.

That was me.

I mentioned it to my regular doctor and she suggested Miralax.

At first, it worked beautifully.

I would mix a capful into my coffee in the morning and usually sometime before lunch I would have a bowel movement.

I thought I had solved it.

After a while though, it became less predictable.

Some mornings it worked.

Some mornings it did not.

Then came fiber gummies. Prunes. Chia seeds. More water. Warm water. Coffee. One of those little stools you put under your feet while you are on the toilet.

Miralax in the morning. Fiber with lunch. Something stronger when I got badly backed up.

Almost every time.

After almost eight years of taking something just to poop...

I sat in a gastroenterologist's office at 63 years old convinced she was about to tell me I had permanently damaged my colon.

That I had made it lazy.

That after years of Miralax, stool softeners, fiber and the occasional Dulcolax when I got desperate, my body had simply forgotten how to go on its own.

I had spent almost a year quietly worrying about it.

What she told me instead changed the way I looked at constipation completely.

And if you have been using something to make yourself go for years, especially if it seems like you need more help now than you used to, I think you will understand why I was so scared.

My name is Patricia.

I am 63 years old.

I have been married to my husband Michael for 37 years.

We have two daughters and four grandchildren.

My life is pretty ordinary.

I walk most mornings.

I garden when my knees cooperate.

I probably eat more bread than I should.

And until my late 50s, I never imagined I would spend so much of my life thinking about bowel movements.

It started around menopause.

At first I simply stopped going every morning.

Then it became every other day.

Then every third day.

Then came the little hard pellets.

If you deal with constipation, you know exactly what I am talking about.

You sit there for twenty minutes.

You push.

Maybe two or three little dry pieces finally come out.

Technically you went.

But you stand up feeling almost exactly as full as you did before.

That was me.

I mentioned it to my regular doctor and she suggested Miralax.

At first, it worked beautifully.

I would mix a capful into my coffee in the morning and usually sometime before lunch I would have a bowel movement.

I thought I had solved it.

After a while though, it became less predictable.

Some mornings it worked.

Some mornings it did not.

Then came fiber gummies. Prunes. Chia seeds. More water. Warm water. Coffee. One of those little stools you put under your feet while you are on the toilet.

And on the really bad weeks, Dulcolax.

I hated Dulcolax.

For me it would do absolutely nothing for hours, then sometime in the middle of the night I would wake up sweating with horrible cramps and spend the next hour in the bathroom.

At least I would finally go.

But three or four days later I would be right back where I started.

Bloated. Heavy. Passing little hard pieces. Never really feeling empty.

Eventually constipation became something I managed every single day.

Miralax in the morning. Fiber with lunch. Something stronger when I got badly backed up.

And for years I told myself that was simply how my body worked now.

Then one night I made the mistake of Googling:

"Can laxatives make your colon lazy?"

I wish I had not.

That one search sent me down a rabbit hole.

I found women saying they could not poop at all anymore unless they took something.

I read about slow transit. Colonic inertia. Impactions. Enemas. Surgery.

By about 3 in the morning I had convinced myself that I had ruined my own digestive system.

And once that thought got into my head, I could not shake it.

Every time Miralax did not work, I wondered if my colon was getting weaker.

Every time I needed Dulcolax, I wondered what I would do when that stopped working too.

That was the question that frightened me most.

What comes after this?

What happens when Miralax is not enough?

What happens when nothing is enough?

What happens when I am 70 and nothing works?

I also realized something that bothered me more than I expected.

I genuinely could not remember the last time I had simply felt a normal urge, gone to the bathroom, and had an easy bowel movement.

Everything had become something I had to manage.

I eventually brought all of this up with my regular doctor.

My bloodwork looked fine. My colonoscopy had been normal.

She told me constipation becomes more common as women get older.

Then came the same advice I had heard for years.

Keep using the Miralax. Drink plenty of water. Make sure you are eating enough fiber.

She was not rude about it.

But I left feeling defeated because I was already doing all of that.

I carried a water bottle around all day and somehow my poop still came out looking like it had been left in the sun.

Fiber often just made me feel more stuffed.

Miralax might give me one decent bowel movement and then two days later I would be back to rabbit pellets.

Nobody could tell me why.

A few months later I went four days with almost nothing despite everything I had taken.

I woke up one morning and my lower stomach felt hard and heavy.

Michael found me lying in bed with my hand over my abdomen.

He asked what was wrong.

And for the first time I actually said the fear out loud.

"I think I have broken my colon."

He knew I struggled with constipation. He had no idea how scared I had become.

That morning he told me we were going to find somebody who actually dealt with this all day instead of adding another bottle to my bathroom cabinet.

A few weeks later, I was sitting across from a gastroenterologist who spent a large part of her practice working with women with chronic constipation.

I went into that appointment expecting bad news.

Instead, she started asking questions about something no doctor had ever spent much time asking me about.

The poop itself.

What did it look like?

Usually little hard pellets.

Did I strain?

Almost every time.

Did I feel empty afterward?

Rarely.

Did increasing fiber help?

Not particularly.

Then she asked:

"When you do go, is the stool usually soft?"

I almost laughed.

No. Most of the time it was dry and hard. Sometimes little pebbles. Sometimes one bigger piece that felt like I was trying to pass a rock.

She pulled out a pad of paper.

Then she said something that reframed everything.

"Everybody focuses on how hard the colon is pushing. But that is rarely the problem. The problem is usually what has happened to the environment inside the colon."

She explained that a healthy colon has a thin mucus lining on the inside of its wall, produced by tiny cells called goblet cells.

That lining does two things.

It coats stool and helps it hold moisture so it stays soft and formed instead of drying into rock.

And it makes the inner wall of the colon slippery, so when the muscle contracts, stool actually glides forward instead of grinding against a dry surface.

She said: "When that lining is healthy, most women go every morning without even thinking about it."

Then she asked me something that stopped me cold.

"Did your constipation start around menopause?"

Yes. Absolutely.

She nodded like she had been expecting that answer.

She explained that estrogen directly feeds goblet cells and signals them to keep producing mucus. When estrogen drops during menopause, those cells lose their signal and mucus production collapses.

She said the same hormonal shift that dries out a woman's skin, eyes, and mouth after 50 also dries out the inside of the colon.

"You just cannot see it because it is happening inside your body."

Then she drew two shapes on the paper. A soft oval and a small hard circle.

She pointed to the first one.

"Imagine squeezing toothpaste through a tube."

Then she pointed at the second.

"Now imagine trying to push a dried-out cork through the same tube."

That was probably the first time constipation had been explained to me in a way that matched what I was actually experiencing.

For years I had assumed my colon was not pushing hard enough. So every time I got constipated, my instinct was to make it push harder. Another laxative. Something stronger.

But nobody had ever asked what condition the stool was in by the time my body was trying to move it. Or what had happened to the lining that was supposed to keep it soft.

Then I asked her something that had bothered me for years.

"If the problem is moisture, why am I still constipated when I drink water all day?"

She told me that was exactly the right question.

The water you drink does not travel through your body and soak the hard stool sitting at the other end of your digestive tract. Most of it is absorbed into your bloodstream much earlier and used throughout the body.

Meanwhile, your colon continues pulling moisture out of the stool already sitting there.

And without that mucus lining to regulate the process, it pulls out too much. The stool dries into cement. And no amount of drinking water changes that because the water never reaches where the problem is.

Then she explained why fiber had made me feel worse.

"Fiber creates bulk. But bulk only helps when there is enough moisture and lubrication to move it. If the lining is gone and the stool is already dry, adding more bulk is like adding more cars to a traffic jam. You are making the blockage bigger, not smaller."

I sat there thinking about every scoop of Metamucil I had choked down over the past six years.

Then she told me what she actually recommended for women in my situation.

She said there were three things my colon needed, and each one handled a different part of the problem.

The first was triphala extract.

She explained that triphala stimulates goblet cells directly and helps them start producing mucus again, even without the estrogen signal they used to depend on. She said research had found it restored the intestinal lining with effects on par with a prescription drug.

She told me this was the root cause piece. Without rebuilding the mucus lining, everything else was temporary.

The second was magnesium oxide.

She explained that this specific form of magnesium stays in the lower bowel instead of absorbing into the bloodstream like citrate or glycinate. Because it stays in the gut, it draws water directly toward the stool that has dried out and compacted.

She said: "Most magnesium supplements are designed to get into your blood. This one is useful precisely because it does not. It stays where the problem is."

The third was kiwifruit extract.

She said bringing water into the bowel was only half the job. If that moisture was not held inside the stool, the colon would just pull it right back out through the damaged wall.

Kiwifruit binds water into the stool at the gel level. She used a sponge as an example.

Pour water onto the counter and it runs everywhere. Put it into a sponge and the sponge holds onto it.

That was how she wanted me to think about magnesium oxide and kiwifruit together.

Magnesium brings the water in. Kiwifruit keeps the stool soft and hydrated instead of letting it turn right back into dry little rocks.

By the time she finished, she had three ingredients written on the page:

Triphala extract.

Magnesium oxide.

Kiwifruit extract.

Next to them she had written:

Rebuild the lining.

Bring water in.

Keep the stool soft.

I looked at the paper for a second and asked:

"Okay... where do I actually get these?"

She smiled.

"Funny enough, my sister takes a formula with all three."

That got my attention.

Her sister was in her late 50s and apparently had dealt with almost exactly what I was describing. Hard stools. Going every few days. That constant feeling that she had not completely finished.

So my gastroenterologist had explained the same three ingredients to her.

Her sister eventually found them together in one formula and had apparently been doing really well with it.

I asked what it was called.

She picked up her phone and searched through her messages for a moment.

Then she turned the screen toward me.

Regularity Reset.

"That is the one my sister takes," she said. "She has done really well with it."

Then she looked back at the three ingredients she had written down for me.

"If you want to try this approach, that is the formula I would look at."

She said what she liked about the combination was that each ingredient handled a different part of the problem.

The triphala rebuilds the mucus lining that menopause took away.

The magnesium oxide brings water directly to the stool.

And the kiwifruit holds that moisture in so the stool stays soft.

After everything she had just explained, it made perfect sense.

I also finally had a very different explanation for what had been happening to me than:

"You destroyed your colon."

My colon was not lazy. It was not broken. It was dry. The lining had disappeared after menopause and nobody had mentioned it until today.

I drove home with that little piece of paper sitting in my handbag.

That evening I looked up Regularity Reset.

Sure enough, the label had exactly what she had written down.

Triphala extract 300 mg. Magnesium oxide 500 mg. Kiwifruit extract 500 mg.

Everything matched what she had spent that appointment explaining to me.

For once, I actually knew why each ingredient was there instead of taking something because somebody on Facebook said it would "make me go."

So I ordered a bottle.

When it arrived, the directions said to take three capsules at night.

I started that evening.

I did not suddenly change everything else I had been doing for years. I was far too nervous for that.

I simply started taking the three capsules consistently and paid attention to what happened.

A few mornings later I noticed the first difference.

The stool itself was softer.

And I know that does not sound terribly exciting.

But after years of passing dry little pellets, it was the exact difference I had been hoping for.

It was formed, but it passed much more easily. I was not sitting there for twenty minutes trying to force something out of me.

Over the next week, that started happening more consistently.

Going to the bathroom gradually stopped feeling like such a production. I could sit down, go, and get on with my morning without all the straining I had gotten used to.

Then sometime during the second week, I was standing in the kitchen making coffee when I felt a normal urge.

That surprised me.

I was not painfully full and trying to make myself go because I knew it had been three days.

I simply needed the bathroom.

I went upstairs, had a bowel movement, and came back down to finish making coffee.

Michael asked why I looked so pleased with myself.

I said:

"I just went without having to think about it first."

He did not really understand why that was such a big deal. But I did.

By the third week, I noticed the heavy feeling in my lower stomach had eased too.

For years my pants would fit fine in the morning and feel tight by dinner.

If I had not gone in a couple of days, I would sometimes eat less because I hated thinking about adding more food on top of everything already sitting inside me.

I was not doing that anymore.

And when I did have a bowel movement, I was finally starting to get something I had almost forgotten about.

That feeling of being finished.

One Saturday morning I went to the bathroom and afterward my stomach just felt light.

There was not that familiar pressure telling me there was still more sitting there.

I walked into the kitchen and told Michael:

"I think I just pooped like a normal person."

He looked over his coffee.

"Well, congratulations."

I laughed.

But honestly, I was emotional about it.

Because people who do not deal with chronic constipation have no idea how much space it takes up in your head.

You know how many days it has been.

You think about whether you should eat a big dinner.

You wonder what you should take before bed.

And when it goes on for years, you start wondering what is going to happen as you get older.

Once I understood that the mucus lining had dried up after menopause, and that fiber was packing a dry pipe tighter, and that laxatives were destroying the goblet cells that could rebuild it, the whole problem finally made sense.

That is why the little note she wrote that day has stuck in my head.

content.body:
They had to remove 14 days of impacted stool by hand at the ER.

If you're chronically constipated, please read this before you end up like me.

I hadn't gone to the bathroom in 14 days.

I told my husband I was fine.

I took another Miralax, then a Senna, then two Dulcolax, and washed it all down with a bottle of magnesium citrate the size of a small soda.

Nothing.

By day 15, I was doubled over on the bathroom floor, unable to stand up from the pressure in my abdomen.

That's when my husband Robert picked me up off the cold tile, carried me to our SUV in nothing but a robe, and drove me to the ER at 2:47 in the morning.

What the doctor said next, about WHY my bowels had stopped working completely, changed everything I thought I knew about my body.

And it's the reason I'm writing this post tonight.

Because if you're a woman over 45 who has been silently struggling with constipation, straining, bloating, or that backed up and heavy feeling like there's still something inside you at the end of every day...

Please read this all the way through.

What I'm about to share with you is the same information that turned my life around in 4 weeks, and it could save yours too.

My name is Margaret. I'm 52 years old. I live in suburban Pennsylvania with my husband Robert.

And like a lot of women my age, I've been quietly battling a constipation problem for years.

It started in my early 40s, around the time I went into perimenopause. Just little things at first. Going every other day instead of every day. Some bloating after dinner. A little discomfort.

But by 47, I was barely going twice a week.

By 49, I was on Miralax every single morning just to function.

And by 51, I was doing everything you can imagine to get my bowels to move.

I had tried EVERYTHING. All the laxatives. The teas. The prune juice. A gallon of water a day. 30 grams of fiber. Digestive enzymes. Probiotics. You name it, I'd taken it.

Nothing was working.

I had two gastroenterologists tell me I had "IBS-C" and to "just keep taking the Miralax."

A third told me my colon was "redundant" and "kinked" and there was nothing to be done.

A fourth ordered a colonoscopy that came back completely normal.

And in the meantime, I was getting worse.

I felt backed up and heavy all the time, like there was something sitting inside me that would not come out no matter what I did. My lower stomach was hard and swollen by the afternoon, and I couldn't take a proper deep breath after dinner.

The brain fog had gotten so bad I'd forget words mid sentence. I had a constant low grade headache that no one could explain.

I was waking up at 3am with this terrible, gripping anxiety I'd never had before in my life. My joints ached, my energy was gone, and my mood was in the toilet.

I had become a stranger in my own body.

And then came the night that nearly killed me.

It started on a Tuesday. By Friday I realized I hadn't gone since the previous Wednesday. That's 9 days.

I doubled my Miralax. Took a Senna. Drank a quart of warm prune juice.

Saturday morning, still nothing.

Sunday, I added Dulcolax to the mix. I felt some movement, so I sat on the toilet for 45 minutes straining, and a few small hard pellets came out. I told myself I was going.

I wasn't.

By Tuesday of the next week, I was on day 14. My stomach was so distended I couldn't button any of my pants. I felt like I had a bowling ball lodged behind my ribs, and I couldn't take a deep breath without sharp pain.

But I told Robert I was fine.

Because I was so used to suffering through this in silence, I'd lost the ability to admit how bad it had gotten.

Around 2 in the morning, I tried to get out of bed to go to the bathroom and just collapsed.

Robert woke up to me on the floor, pale, sweating, unable to speak. He didn't ask. He just picked me up, wrapped me in a robe, and carried me to the car.

By 3:15am we were in the ER at our local hospital.

By 4am I was on a stretcher, hooked up to an IV, getting wheeled in for an emergency CT scan.

And by 5:30am, the ER doctor, a woman about my age named Dr. Sarah Chen, came to my bed with the scan results in her hand.

She sat down on the edge of the bed and gently told me what they'd found.

I had 14 days of impacted stool packed into my colon. It was so dried out and compacted that no laxative was going to move it. Not anymore.

They were going to have to remove it manually, right there in the hospital.

I couldn't even look at her.

I'm not going to describe what happened next, because it's the most humiliating experience of my life.

But by 8am that morning, the impaction was out. I was exhausted, sore, embarrassed, and I just wanted to go home and never speak of it again.

But before I could leave, Dr. Chen came back into the room.

She pulled up a chair next to my bed, looked me in the eye, and said something I wasn't expecting at all.

"Mrs. Whitman, before you go home, I need you to understand something. The stool we just removed isn't your problem. It's the symptom. There's a reason you've been struggling with constipation for years that no one has ever told you about. And unless you address it, this is going to keep happening for the rest of your life."

I just stared at her.

For the first time in 6 years, a doctor was about to actually explain what was wrong with me.

Dr. Chen took a breath and started from the beginning.

She told me what I had wasn't really "IBS-C." It wasn't a "redundant colon." It wasn't "just menopause."

She said the real problem was much simpler than that.

👉 "Mrs. Whitman, your colon is dry."

I told her that was impossible. I drank more water than anyone I knew, a gallon a day, sometimes more.

She nodded like she'd heard it a thousand times before.

👉 "I believe you, and I'm sure it barely helped, because almost none of that water ever reaches the part of you that needs it. The water you drink gets absorbed high up, in your small intestine and the first stretch of your colon, and from there it goes straight into your bloodstream."

"By the time anything gets down to the far end where your stool is actually sitting and waiting, there's very little left."

I asked her why that mattered so much.

That's when she explained the part that made my jaw drop.

👉 "Because your colon is supposed to have a built-in system for keeping stool wet and moving. And yours has shut down."

She explained that the inside of a healthy colon is lined with a thin layer of mucus. A slippery, protective coating produced by tiny cells called goblet cells.

That mucus lining does two things that nothing else in the body can do.

It coats the stool and helps it hold moisture, keeping it soft and formed instead of drying into rock.

And it makes the colon wall slippery, so when the muscle contracts, stool actually glides forward instead of grinding against a dry surface.

"When that lining is healthy," she said, "most women go every morning without ever thinking about it. The stool is soft, it slides, and the whole thing takes three minutes."

"When it disappears, your colon becomes a bare dry pipe. And a bare dry pipe does one thing extremely well: it sucks every last drop of moisture out of whatever is sitting inside it."

"Hour after hour. Day after day. Until your stool has the consistency of concrete."

I felt my chest tighten.

She was describing exactly what I had been living with.

Then she asked me the question that connected everything.

👉 "When did your constipation start getting really bad?"

I told her it was around 46, 47. Right around perimenopause.

She nodded like she'd been expecting that answer.

👉 "That's because estrogen is what feeds your goblet cells. It's the signal that tells them to keep producing mucus. When estrogen drops during menopause, those cells lose their signal and mucus production collapses."

"The same hormonal shift that dried out your skin after 50. Your eyes. Your mouth. It dried out the inside of your colon too."

"You just couldn't see it because it was happening inside your body."

I sat there doing the math. My skin had gotten dry around the same time. My eyes too. I'd started using eye drops and heavier moisturizer right around 47.

My colon had been drying out at the exact same time and nobody had ever connected it.

Not one of my four gastroenterologists. Not my gynecologist. Nobody.

Then Dr. Chen explained the part that made me furious.

👉 "And while menopause was drying your colon out from one direction, the products you were taking to fix it were destroying it from the other direction."

She told me that stimulant laxatives like senna and Dulcolax do not soften stool. They do not add moisture. What they do is dump a chemical irritant onto the colon wall that is so aggressive that the muscle goes into emergency spasms.

"That cramping you feel after Dulcolax? That is not a bowel movement. That is your colon's panic response to a chemical burn."

"And every single dose destroys more goblet cells. The same cells that produce the mucus lining you already don't have enough of."

She told me a study found visible colon wall damage in 81% of women who used stimulant laxatives for just 12 months.

I had been using them on and off for nearly five years.

👉 "So menopause took the lining from one side. And the laxatives you took to cope with the constipation destroyed what was left from the other side."

"Every dose made your colon drier. Every box of senna made the next month worse. And you kept needing more because the product was creating the condition that sold more of the product."

I sat there in that hospital gown and felt sick.

Because I realized I had been paying to accelerate the destruction of my own colon for five years. And I thought I was helping myself.

Then she explained why fiber had made me worse too.

👉 "Fiber creates bulk. That's all it does. It makes the stool bigger."

"If your colon had moisture and a healthy lining, more bulk would help move things along."

"But you're adding dry bulk to a colon that has no moisture barrier left. You're making the plug bigger and drier. More cars into a traffic jam."

I thought about every scoop of Metamucil, every fiber gummy, every chia seed smoothie I had choked down for six years while getting progressively worse.

More fiber. More bloating. More pressure. Bigger blockage.

Nobody had ever explained why.

I asked Dr. Chen the obvious question. "So how do I fix this?"

She told me that to actually solve the root cause, three things had to happen.

✅ First, the mucus lining had to be rebuilt.

This was the root cause piece. Without restoring the goblet cells and getting them producing mucus again, everything else was temporary.

She told me about a fruit extract called triphala that stimulates goblet cells directly and triggers them to start producing mucus again, even without the estrogen signal they used to depend on.

"Research found it restored the intestinal lining with effects on par with a prescription drug," she said. "And it doesn't irritate the colon wall the way laxatives do. It rebuilds what laxatives and menopause destroyed."

✅ Second, water had to be pulled directly into the colon where the stool is.

Not more water in my mouth that gets absorbed into my bloodstream before it ever reaches the problem. Actual water drawn osmotically into the lower bowel.

She told me the mineral that does this is magnesium oxide.

"Most magnesium supplements are designed to get into your blood," she said. "Citrate, glycinate, they absorb quickly and leave the gut. Great for sleep. Useless for a dry colon."

"Magnesium oxide is different. It absorbs poorly, and for constipation that is the entire point. It stays in the lower bowel and draws water directly toward the stool that has dried into rock."

✅ Third, that water had to be locked inside the stool so the colon couldn't strip it back out.

"This is the piece most people miss," she said. "You can flood the colon with water, but if it just sits loose around the stool, your colon wall sucks it right back out within hours and you're dry again by tomorrow."

She told me kiwifruit extract binds water directly into the stool at the gel level and holds it there. Like a sponge.

"Pour water on the counter and it runs everywhere. Put it into a sponge and the sponge holds onto it."

"That's how magnesium oxide and kiwifruit work together. Magnesium brings the water in. Kiwifruit pulls it inside the stool and keeps it there so it stays soft the entire way down."

She told me a clinical trial found kiwifruit outperformed psyllium fiber and produced 1.5 extra complete bowel movements per week.

By the time she finished, she had three ingredients written on a hospital notepad:

Triphala extract. Magnesium oxide. Kiwifruit extract.

Next to them she'd written:

Rebuild the lining. Bring water in. Keep the stool soft.

I asked her where I could get all three.

👉 "You can buy them separately," she said. "But quite a few of my patients take one called Regularity Reset because it combines all three at the right doses in one capsule. You're not standing in your kitchen every night trying to measure out three different things."

She wrote the name on the notepad and slid it across the bed.

"500mg of magnesium oxide to flood the dry colon with water. 500mg of kiwifruit extract to pull that water inside the stool and hold it there. And 300mg of triphala extract to rebuild the goblet cells and restore the mucus lining that menopause took away."

"It's a small company and they only sell on their own website. Fair warning, they run out of stock fairly often."

I didn't even change out of the hospital clothes. I sat down at the kitchen table, pulled up the website on my phone, and ordered a bottle of Regularity Reset right then and there.

By the fourth morning, I had my first complete bowel movement in years, without a laxative.

And it was soft. I didn't strain, I didn't brace myself, I didn't grab onto anything. It simply came out.

I sat there for a long time afterwards just trying to take it in. Robert knocked on the door to check on me. All I could tell him was that I'd gone.
